content: When redistributing zidovudine (AZT)-based and nevirapine (NVP)-based regimens, healthcare providers must carefully manage their stock to prevent shortages or wastage due to product expiration from overstocking. Initial demand for alternative first-line, second-line, or third-line regimens, particularly those containing newer medications like dolutegravir (DTG), darunavir/ritonavir (DRV/r), and raltegravir (RAL), may be limited. To address this, pooling orders from multiple buyers is recommended to increase order volumes, ensuring suppliers can meet demand effectively. Transitioning to preferred regimens and formulations, such as tenofovir disoproxil fumarate (TDF)and efavirenz (EFV)-based products, requires careful planning and coordination with suppliers to determine the pace at which increased quantities can be made available. A phased approach to this transition is essential, incorporating the test and offer paradigm and alternative scale-up targets. Programs should initiate new patients eligible for antiretroviral therapy (ART) on TDF-based regimens, prioritizing fixed-dose combinations (FDCs) like TDF + lamivudine (3TC) + EFV or TDF + emtricitabine (FTC) + EFV. Buffer stocks should be included in supply plans, and close collaboration with suppliers and procurement mechanisms is necessary to understand global demand patterns and act accordingly. Procurement of stavudine (d4T) should cease due to its cumulative mitochondrial toxicity. Patients currently on d4T-based regimens should transition to TDF-based regimens. Similarly, didanosine (ddI) should no longer be procured, as it is no longer recommended as an alternative nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor (NRTI) in adult and adolescent second-line regimens due to its toxicity, lower efficacy, and inconvenient dosing requirements. Patients on first-line AZTand/or NVP-based regimens should be transitioned to preferred first-line FDCs in a phased manner, considering the speed at which TDF products can be ordered and delivered. In regions with high HIV-2 prevalence, formulations with two-drug FDCs (e.g., TDF with 3TC, TDF with FTC, or AZT with 3TC) may be preferred, as they allow flexibility to combine the NRTI backbone with protease inhibitors (PIs) or integrase strand transfer inhibitors (INSTIs) for firstand second-line therapy. For secondor third-line regimens, procurement managers should consider pooling demand with other domestic programs, neighboring countries, or regional initiatives to meet manufacturers’ production batch sizes. Where feasible, larger buffer stocks should be held for essential products in low demand, and initial orders for newly introduced products may require longer lead times. Supply chain considerations for implementing less frequent ART drug refills, community ART delivery, and lay providers distributing ART drugs include examining the current supply chain model and its performance. Local supply chains must be agile enough to support various service delivery models, including community-level care. A phased approach should account for additional ARV drugs needed at pickup sites, the number of patients served by multi-month prescriptions, local storage capacity, additional reporting requirements, ARV drug shelf-life constraints, and overall supply chain performance. National programs should limit pediatric ARV drug procurement to formulations listed in the Optimal Pediatric Formulary of the Inter-Agency Task Team (IATT) on Prevention and Treatment of HIV Infection in Pregnant Women, Mothers, and Their Children. This simplifies the supply chain and stabilizes the global supply of pediatric ARV drugs. Stavudine (d4T) and didanosine (ddI) should no longer be procured for pediatric use due to toxicity and other limitations. Age-appropriate FDCs, particularly dispersible tablets, are preferred over oral liquid formulations. When introducing new products, policymakers and procurement managers must consider intellectual property restrictions, product registration status, forecasted demand, and the impact on existing medicines or diagnostics. Accurate forecasting is challenging, and procurement plans must account for potential adoption rates to avoid stock-outs or wastage. Collaboration with suppliers to adjust delivery schedules based on demand is essential. For products in low demand, pooled procurement with neighboring countries or global mechanisms may be necessary to meet viable order volumes. Strategic planning for laboratory and diagnostic services is critical to ensure accurate and reliable testing. This includes strengthening laboratory networks, increasing access to CD4 count and viral load testing, supporting point-of-care diagnostics, and ensuring high-quality diagnostic tools. Leadership and governance are essential to expand services, train healthcare workers, and implement quality assurance systems.
